issues.legal_issue: A director’s allotment of additional shares to himself is invalid and oppressive when it is unauthorized, unnecessary for the company, or made for the improper purpose of obtaining control.
material_facts: The managing director purported to allot additional shares to himself, converting the existing majority shareholders into minority shareholders.
The other director denied attending the meeting said to have approved the first allotment, and no notice of the meeting or attendance record was produced.
The company’s records did not establish a need for the additional funds or show how the alleged advance was used.
The managing director did not establish that the allotments were made in the company’s interests or in accordance with proper procedure; the evidence indicated that the purpose was to gain control.
issues.conclusion: The allotments were unauthorized, fraudulent and oppressive, and were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Directors act in a fiduciary capacity and must act in good faith, make full and honest disclosure, and exercise the power to issue shares for a proper purpose and in the interests of the company. An individual director cannot exercise a power reserved to the board. These duties apply to private companies even though Section 81 of the Companies Act, 1956 does not apply to them. An allotment made to secure or maintain control for the directors’ own benefit may be set aside. The Court relied on Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956; the company’s Articles of Association; Regal (Hastings) Ltd. v. Gulliver; Alexander v. Automatic Telephone Co.; Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.; Punt v. Symons; Piercy v. S. Mills & Co. Ltd.; Hogg v. Cramphorn Ltd.; Howard Smith Ltd. v. Ampol Petroleum Ltd.; Rolled Steel Products (Holdings) Ltd. v. British Steel Corporation; Bishopsgate Investment Management Ltd. v. Maxwell; Whitehouse v. Carlton Hotel Pty. Ltd.; and Tea Brokers (P) Ltd. v. Hemendra Prosad Barooah.

rule.if: company_oppression_proceeding and director_allotted_shares_to_self and (no_valid_board_approval or no_company_need_for_funds or allotment_made_to_obtain_control)

predicates.company_oppression_proceeding: A proceeding was brought alleging oppression in the management of a company.
predicates.director_allotted_shares_to_self: A director caused additional company shares to be allotted to himself.
predicates.no_valid_board_approval: The alleged board approval was not established as a valid decision of the board.
predicates.no_company_need_for_funds: The company’s circumstances did not establish a need for the additional funds purportedly raised by the allotment.
predicates.allotment_made_to_obtain_control: The director used the allotment to obtain or maintain control of the company for himself.

issues.definition: When a director allots shares to himself in an oppression proceeding and valid approval is absent, the company needs no funds, or the allotment is made to obtain control, the allotment is set aside.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of prior regulatory permission for a share transfer does not by itself defeat the transfer where permission may be obtained after the event.
material_facts: The shares were transferred to the petitioners and the company entered the transfer in its register of members, although prior permission had not been obtained.
The managing director had proposed the arrangement under which the shares were acquired and transferred.
The governing statute imposed no time limit for obtaining permission, and the replacement statute did not contain the same requirement.
issues.conclusion: The lack of prior permission did not invalidate the transfer; permission could be obtained after the event.
issues.legal_principle: Permission under Section 29 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 could be obtained ex post facto because the statute prescribed no time limit. The Court relied on Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Escorts Ltd. and noted that the Foreign Exchange Management Act, which replaced FERA, did not contain the same requirement.

predicates.share_transfer_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a transfer of company shares is effective despite a regulatory permission issue.
predicates.prior_permission_not_obtained: The required permission had not been obtained before the share transfer.
predicates.post_event_permission_available: The governing legal framework permitted the relevant permission to be obtained after the transfer.

issues.definition: When a share-transfer dispute involves missing prior permission but permits permission after the event, the transfer is not invalidated solely for lack of prior permission.

issues.legal_issue: Shareholders who satisfy the statutory qualification when they file an oppression petition have standing to maintain it when they are registered members of the company.
material_facts: The petitioners were recorded as shareholders in the company’s register of members when they filed their petition.
They held the requisite number of shares to bring the petition.
The managing director had caused the company to record the transfers and later challenged the petitioners’ standing on the basis of the permission issue.
issues.conclusion: The petitioners had standing to maintain the petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956.
issues.legal_principle: The required shareholder qualification is assessed when the proceeding is instituted; later events do not undo standing that existed at filing. The Court relied on Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956, Rajahmundry Electric Supply Corporation Ltd. v. A. Nageshwara Rao, S. Varadarajan v. Venkateshwara Solvent Extraction (P) Ltd., and Jawahar Singh Bikram Singh v. Sharda Talwar.

predicates.company_oppression_petition: The proceeding is a petition alleging oppression or mismanagement of a company.
predicates.petitioners_registered_as_members_at_fil: The petitioners were recorded as company members when they filed the petition.
predicates.requisite_shareholding_at_filing: The petitioners held the required share qualification when they filed the petition.

issues.definition: When an oppression petition is filed by registered members who then hold the required share qualification, the petitioners have standing to maintain it.

issues.legal_issue: In an appeal confined to questions of law, a High Court may set aside a factual finding that is perverse or unsupported by evidence.
material_facts: The appeal to the High Court was brought under Section 10F of the Companies Act, 1956, which provides for an appeal on a question of law.
The Company Law Board had reached its decision cursorily and had not addressed relevant issues concerning the alleged share allotments.
The High Court examined the record and gave fuller reasons concerning the allotments and alleged oppression.
issues.conclusion: The High Court did not exceed its jurisdiction by addressing the factual findings because their perversity raised a question of law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10F of the Companies Act, 1956 limits an appeal to questions of law, but a finding that is perverse or based on no evidence raises a question of law and may be set aside on appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_company_law_board: The proceeding is an appeal from a decision of the Company Law Board.
predicates.appeal_limited_to_questions_of_law: The appeal is limited by law to questions of law.
predicates.factual_finding_perverse_or_without_evid: The challenged factual finding is perverse or has no evidentiary support.

issues.definition: When an appeal from the Company Law Board is limited to questions of law, a perverse or unsupported factual finding may be set aside by the High Court.

issues.legal_issue: A majority shareholder reduced to a minority through an oppressive and fraudulent share allotment should not be required to sell shares to the wrongdoer as a remedy.
material_facts: The managing director’s allotments to himself reduced the petitioners, who had been majority shareholders, to minority shareholders.
The allotments were found to be fraudulent and oppressive, and the managing director had gained an advantage through his conduct.
The Company Law Board had allowed the petitioners to sell their shares to the managing director, while the High Court set aside the allotments.
issues.conclusion: Setting aside the impugned allotments was proper; requiring the oppressed shareholders to sell their shares to the wrongdoer would reward the wrongdoer and fail to redress the oppression.
issues.legal_principle: Relief for oppression depends on the circumstances of the case and should undo the advantage gained through the oppressive conduct rather than impose a remedy that rewards the wrongdoer or penalizes the oppressed party. The Court applied Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 and relied on the principles discussed in Tea Brokers (P) Ltd. v. Hemendra Prosad Barooah.

predicates.company_oppression_proceeding: The proceeding seeks relief for oppression in a company.
predicates.majority_shareholder_reduced_to_minority: A share allotment made oppressively reduced a majority shareholder to a minority shareholder.
predicates.wrongdoer_gained_control: The person responsible for the oppressive conduct gained control or another advantage from it.

issues.definition: When an oppressive allotment reduces a majority shareholder to a minority and benefits the wrongdoer, the allotment is set aside and the oppressed shareholder is not required to sell to that person.
